X = macro_predictors.drop(columns=['month', 'rp_div']).values

# OLS for Welsh data fails because X is not of full rank
print(X.shape[1], np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))




As for OLS, the objective function is to minimize the sum of squared errors \((y - X\beta)'(y - X\beta)\) under the condition that \(\sum\limits_{j=2}^K \beta_j \leq t(\lambda)\) if an intercept is present. This can be rewritten as \(\beta'A\beta \leq t(\lambda)\) where \(A = \begin{pmatrix}0&&\ldots&&0\\\vdots& 1&0&\ldots&0\\&\vdots&\ddots&&0\\0& &\ldots&&1\end{pmatrix}\). Otherwise, the condition is simply that \(\beta'I_K\beta \leq t(\lambda)\) where \(I_k\) is an identity matrix of size (\(k \times k\)).

RPython



ridge_regression <- function(y, X, lambda = 0, intercept = FALSE) {
  K <- ncol(X)
  A <- diag(K)
  if (intercept) {
    A[1, ] <- 0
  }
  coeffs <- solve(t(X) %*% X + lambda * A) %*% t(X) %*% y
  return(coeffs)
}




def ridge_regression(y, X, lambda_=0, intercept=False):
    K = X.shape[1]
    A = np.eye(K)
    if intercept:
        A[0, :] = 0
    coeffs = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lambda_ * A, X.T @ y)
    return coeffs

Note that to implement this evaluation in a tidy manner, vectorized functions are important! seq(from = 0.01, to = 20, by = 0.1) |>

  mutate(norm = l2_norm(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = norm)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Lambda", y = " L2 norm")

    return np.sum(ridge_regression(y, X, lambda_)**2)

l2_norm_vec = np.vectorize(l2_norm)

 .assign(norm=lambda df: l2_norm_vec(df['value']))
 .assign(gg=lambda df: ggplot(aes(x='value', y='norm'), df))
 .gg[0] + geom_line() + labs(x='Lambda', y='L2 norm')
)




To compute the coefficients of linear regression with a penalty on the sum of the absolute value of the regression coefficients, numerical optimization routines are required. Recall, the objective function is to minimize the sum of squared residuals, \(\hat\varepsilon'\hat\varepsilon\) under the constraint that \(\sum\limits_{j=2}^K\beta_j\leq t(\lambda)\). Make sure you familiarize yourself with the way, numerical optimization in R works: we first define the objective function (objective_lasso()) which has the parameter we aim to optimize as its first argument. The main function lasso_regression() then only calls this helper function.

RPython



objective_lasso <- function(beta, y, X, lambda, intercept) {
  residuals <- y - X %*% beta
  sse <- sum(residuals^2)
  penalty <- sum(abs(beta))
  if (intercept) {
    penalty <- penalty - abs(beta[1])
  }
  return(sse + lambda * penalty)
}

lasso_regression <- function(y, X, lambda = 0, intercept = FALSE) {
  K <- ncol(X)
  beta_init <- rep(0, K)
  return(optim(par = beta_init, fn = objective_lasso, y = y, X = X, lambda = lambda, intercept = intercept)$par)
}

rc <- c(NA, lasso_regression(y, X, lambda = 0.01))

# Add an intercept term
rc_i <- lasso_regression(y, cbind(1, X), lambda = 0.01, intercept = TRUE)
cbind(rc, rc_i)




def objective_lasso(beta, y, X, lambda_, intercept):
    residuals = y - np.dot(X, beta)
    sse = np.sum(residuals**2)
    penalty = np.sum(np.abs(beta))
    if intercept:
        penalty -= np.abs(beta[0])
    return sse + lambda_ * penalty

def lasso_regression(y, X, lambda_=0, intercept=False):
    K = X.shape[1]
    beta_init = np.zeros(K)
    result = minimize(objective_lasso, beta_init, args=(y, X, lambda_, intercept))
    return result.x

# Without intercept
rc = np.concatenate(([np.nan], lasso_regression(y, X, lambda_=0.01)))

# With intercept
rc_i = lasso_regression(y, np.column_stack((np.ones(len(y)), X)), lambda_=0.01, intercept=True)

np.column_stack((rc, rc_i))

(pd.DataFrame({'value': np.arange(0, 0.51, 0.05)})

)

title: Portfolio Choice under Transaction Costs
text:
In this exercise, we substantially extend the simple portfolio analysis and bring the simulation closer to a realistic framework. We will penalize turnover, evaluate the out-of-sample performance after transaction costs and introduce some robust optimization procedures in the spirit of the paper Large-scale portfolio allocation under transaction costs and model uncertainty, available in Absalon. We start with standard mean-variance efficient portfolios. Then, we introduce further constraints step-by-step. Numerical constrained optimization is performed by the packages quadprog (for quadratic objective functions such as in typical mean-variance framework) and alabama (for more general, non-linear objectives and constraints). I refer to Exercise Set Portfolio Choice Problems for a basic introduction into numerical optimization, etc.
Exercises:

You will use the monthly Fama-French industry portfolio returns for the exercise set. Download them directly from Kenneth French’s homepage or load them from the parquet files.
Write a function that computes efficient portfolio weight allowing for \(L_2\) transaction costs (conditional on the holdings before reallocation). \(L_2\) transaction costs mean that within this exercise, we assume that transaction costs are quadratic and of the form \[\frac{\beta}{2}\left(w_{t+1} - w_{t^+}\right)'\left(w_{t+1} - w_{t^+}\right).\]. Thus, the function should take the sample estimates \(\hat\mu_t\) and \(\hat\Sigma_t\), the previous portfolio weight \(\omega_{t^+} := \frac{\omega_{t} \odot \left(1 + r_t\right)}{1 + w_t'r_t}\) where \(\odot\) denotes element-wise multiplication as well as the transaction cost parameter \(\beta\) and the risk aversion \(\gamma\) as inputs. You can consult Equation (7) in Hautsch et al. (2019) for further information. Compute the efficient portfolio for an arbitrary initial portfolio based on the industry returns.
Analyse how different transaction cost values \(\beta\) affect portfolio rebalancing. You can assume that the previous allocation was the naive portfolio. Show that for high values of \(\beta\). The initial portfolio becomes more relevant. What happens for different values of the risk aversion \(\gamma\)?
Write a script that simulates the performance of 3 different strategies before and after adjusting for transaction costs for different values of \(\beta\) with \(L_1\) transaction costs: A (mean-variance) utility maximization (risk aversion \(\gamma = 4\)), a naive allocation that rebalances daily and a (mean-variance) utility with turnover adjustment (risk aversion \(\gamma = 4\)). Assume that \(\beta = 1\). Evaluate the out-of-sample mean, standard deviation, and Sharpe ratios. What do you conclude about the relevance of turnover penalization?

Solutions:
All solutions are provided in the book chapter Constrained optimization and backtesting.

Prerequisites

Install the required software

Set Up the Course Repository

title: Getting started
text:
When something goes wrong
Every message says what went wrong and what to do, and ends with a code in brackets. A rejected submission lists every problem at once. The most common ones:







Code
Meaning




close_date_in_future
close_date is later than the close before your trade. The message names the date to use.


unknown_ticker
Not a stock in the simulation. It uses Yahoo tickers, for example BRK-B.


ineligible_ticker
Closed below $5. You may hold or reduce such a position, but not add to it.


short_not_allowed
A negative weight before shorting opens on 5 April.


leverage_exceeded, net_exposure_exceeded
The sum of absolute weights, or of weights, is above the limit.


too_many_positions
More than 50 non-zero weights.


rationale_missing
Every submission needs a rationale.


missing_token, unknown_token
No token was found, or the server does not know it: check AEF_TOKEN.



The aefsim README explains every code.

title: The trading simulation
text: Over the semester your team runs a paper portfolio of US stocks. Whenever you like, you send new target weights from R or Python. The simulation trades them at the next US market open, charges transaction costs, and values the portfolio at every close. Your team’s dashboard shows how you are doing against simple benchmarks and the cohort; the public leaderboard shows everyone under pseudonyms.

title: The trading simulation
text:
Teams and timeline

Work alone or in a team of up to three. Each team gets one token and starts with $1,000,000 in cash.
Dry run: 25 January to 5 February 2027, to try the tools; results are reset afterwards.
Trading: 8 February to 14 May 2027, every NYSE trading day.

The rules tighten during the semester. Every response from the simulation tells you which rule set applies to the next trade, so a change never catches you by surprise.








From
Rule set
What changes




8 February
P1
Long only, no transaction costs


1 March
P2
Every trade costs 10 bps of its value


5 April
P3
Short selling allowed: gross exposure up to 160 %, net up to 100 %, borrow fee 50 bps a year



Throughout: at most 50 positions, no limit on a single weight, and gross exposure up to 100 % until shorting opens.

title: The trading simulation
text:
What you can trade
The universe is CRSP’s common stock: ordinary shares of US companies (share codes 10 and 11) listed on NYSE, NYSE American or Nasdaq. ETFs, funds, ADRs and REITs are excluded. Membership comes from CRSP itself, at its latest update, so a stock listed since then can be traded only once CRSP includes it. You can buy a stock if it closed at $5 or more on the day before your trade; get_universe() lists exactly those stocks. If a stock you hold drops below $5, you may keep it or reduce it, but not add to it.
Prices are not part of the simulation’s API. Download them yourself, for example with tidyfinance: it reads the same Yahoo Finance data the simulation trades at.

title: The trading simulation
text:
How a day works

Decide after a US close, with data up to that close. That day is your close_date.
Submit whenever you like. Your weights trade at the next market open whose deadline has not passed: 09:00 New York time on the trading day. That is 15:00 in Copenhagen, except from 15 to 26 March 2027, when the US is already on summer time and the deadline is 14:00. A submission sent after a deadline, over a weekend or before the simulation starts waits for the next open. You may submit as often as you like; the last accepted submission before a deadline is the one that trades. cancel() withdraws a submission until then.
Trade at that day’s opening price. If you submit nothing, your portfolio is left as it is: no trades and no costs.
Mark to market at the close. Results appear the next morning, Copenhagen time.

A submission is a set of target weights: fractions of your portfolio’s value, by ticker. Tickers you leave out are sold, and whatever the weights don’t use stays in cash. The simulation trades fractional shares so that after costs your weights are exactly the targets. If a submission breaks a rule, it is rejected as a whole with error codes saying why, and it still appears in your log. validate() runs the same checks without submitting.

title: The trading simulation
text:
Money, costs and corporate actions

Cash earns SOFR, the US overnight rate, day by day (act/360). Negative cash, which can arise once shorting opens, pays the same rate.
Transaction costs are a fixed fraction of the value traded, in both directions.
Short positions pay the borrow fee on their market value.
Dividends are paid into cash on the ex-date. Short positions pay them.
Stock splits change your share count, not your value.
Delisted stocks are sold at their last price.
A stock with no opening price that day cannot trade, so you keep what you held.
